source.title: Volumization as a Natural Generalization of Weight Decay
source.authors: Liu Ziyin; Zihao Wang; Makoto Yamada; Masahito Ueda

record.file_problem: Full paper text supplied. Some table headings and values are flattened, but Table 2's row order supports assigning its accuracy pairs to the listed methods.
record.tranche_reason: The paper tests performance under varying label-noise rates and argues that volumization can prevent overfitting in noisy-label settings. It does not test the original random-label fitting result directly.
record.gate_note: The paper cites Zhang et al. (2017) for fitting mislabeled data despite augmentation, weight decay and dropout; that cited result is not this study's evidence. Its own noisy-label experiments report test accuracy, not training error. It does not test fully random labels, shuffled or noise inputs, or the learning order of real and noisy labels.
record.test_reason: The study evaluates a proposed regularizer using test accuracy, robustness and quantization performance. It reports neither training-set fitting nor separate learning trajectories for clean and corrupted labels. Its random-label memorization premise comes from cited work; its own results do not establish any listed version.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate but understates the authors' interpretation: they claim volumization improves generalization and prevents memorization, particularly under strong noise, and also supports adversarial robustness and weight quantization. The supplied experiments establish test-performance differences rather than directly measuring prevention of memorization.
record.recipe_differences: Introduces volumization, a weight constraint/regularizer; noisy-label experiments compare it with weight decay and no regularization rather than reproducing random-label memorization tests.
record.method_sensitivity: The authors report that the effect depends on dataset, architecture, noise rate and volumization parameters v and α; stronger noise generally calls for stronger regularization.

fits_no_version.finding: Table 2 reports best and final test accuracies under selected label-noise rates. For ResNet18 on CIFAR10 with 0.8 noise, no regularization yields 39.67% best and 16.67% final accuracy; volumization yields 45.56% and 38.16%. These quantify generalization and mitigation performance, without measuring training-label memorization.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Volumization can improve generalization under substantial label noise in the tested settings.

fits_no_version.finding: Figure 5b attributes the baseline's test-performance decline after epoch 20 to learning mislabeled points. No separate clean-label or corrupted-label fitting measurements establish the proposed temporal mechanism.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Noisy-label training can exhibit an early test-accuracy peak followed by deterioration, which suitable volumization can reduce.

record.problems: For the claim versions, the paper provides no random-label or unstructured-input experiments. Its noisy-label experiments report test accuracy rather than training error, so they do not establish whether the networks fit the corrupted training set. Several trajectory results are figures without tabulated values.
record.rows_left_out: No rows: the study's own results do not report training error or another outcome that establishes the behavior named by V4. Table 2 and Table 3 report test accuracy under label noise only; those values cannot determine whether training sets were fit perfectly.

untested.parts: Fitting completely random labels to near-zero training error, chance test performance, and unchanged architecture and training hyperparameters.
Time required to fit true versus random labels and convergence speed as corruption increases.
Fitting shuffled pixels, independently permuted pixels or Gaussian-noise inputs.
Perfect training-set fitting across corruption fractions and steady test-error degradation toward chance. Selected noise levels have test accuracies, but no corresponding training errors.
Random-label fitting under weight decay, dropout and augmentation, and true-label generalization after their removal. Volumization is a different intervention.
Direct comparison of when clean-label patterns and corrupted labels are learned. Test-accuracy declines alone do not establish that ordering.

record.verdict_notes: The empty result-row set is appropriate for these claim versions. Change the record's V4 status from tested_not_extracted to not_tested. Tables 2–3 are already declared in rows_left_out, so they are not missing results. The cited Zhang et al. finding is not evidence produced by this study.

versions.untested_parts: Whether standard networks fit completely random training labels with chance test error, without changing architecture or hyperparameters.
Training time to fit random labels and how convergence time changes with corruption fraction.
Training on shuffled, permuted or Gaussian-noise inputs.

The paper varies label-noise rates and reports test accuracy, but does not report training-set error. It does not establish perfect fitting at every noise rate or a steady rise in test error toward chance.
Whether weight decay, dropout or augmentation permit fitting random labels, or whether their removal alone harms true-label generalization.
Whether real-label patterns are learned before noisy or random labels.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
